text:
The Data Supply Chain: Why Your Car Is Selling You to Your Insurer

Northeastern University researchers, working with Consumer Reports, tested 21 late-model vehicles and 30 companion mobile apps. The findings, peer-reviewed and published this week, describe something worse than a privacy problem. They describe a functioning supply chain. Vehicles produce data. App developers and advertising networks process it. Data brokers package it. Insurers and banks consume it. The vehicle owner is the only participant who does not know they are in the chain.

The quantitative scope is broad. All 21 vehicles transmitted data to at least one outside domain. Nineteen of the twenty-one sent traffic to a third party. More than half contacted domains classified as advertising, tracking, or analytics. Tesla's Model 3 led with 34 unique ATA domains, followed by the Cybertruck at 23, the Cadillac Lyriq at 10, and the Lucid Air at 9. Seven of the thirty companion apps transmitted sensitive identifiers — the vehicle identification number, email address, phone number, or precise location — directly to advertising and tracking companies. When the researchers paired the companion app to the vehicle, exposure to advertising and tracking companies roughly doubled.

The list of recipients is not a set of obscure data brokers. It includes Adobe, ContentSquare, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Snap, and Yahoo. When the researchers presented their findings to the automakers, all but one deflected. The exception was Honda.

Honda's response is the most consequential single fact in the study. Upon receiving the findings, Honda asked its analytics vendor Amplitude to delete all collected location data and updated its HondaLink app to stop sending geolocation. The vehicle identification number was reclassified from a marketing item to something requiring different treatment. Honda's spokesperson confirmed the changes.

The implication is not that Honda is better than the other eighteen automakers. The implication is that the data flow was a choice, not a technical constraint. Honda had the contractual power to stop Amplitude from collecting location data. It had the technical capacity to update its app. It had the organizational willingness to reclassify a data element. What it did not have, until a research team arrived with packet captures, was a reason to exercise any of those capabilities. The privacy policies that say "we may share information with third parties" were not descriptions of what was technically required. They were descriptions of what the companies had decided to do.

Several automakers offered a different explanation. They said some links within their companion apps opened outside webpages that deployed cookies to collect customer data. The cookie explanation is technically accurate and strategically irrelevant. Whether the data was collected by the vehicle's onboard modem, the app's own code, or a webview cookie, the driver was not informed. The mechanism of collection is an implementation detail. The absence of consent is the product.

The demand side of the supply chain explains why the data keeps flowing. Insurance companies and banks buy the outputs. LexisNexis and Verisk compile driving scores from vehicle telemetry and sell them to auto insurers. One driver's premium rose 50% after LexisNexis obtained her data. Another saw an 80% increase after an automaker shared hundreds of entries with a data broker. GM disclosed in a California privacy filing that it made approximately $20 million over four years selling customer data. The privacy remediation costs, legal exposure, and regulatory penalties are now in the tens of millions. The data revenue is not worth the legal and reputational cost, which explains why automaker interest in data monetization fell 7 percentage points from 2025 to 2026.

The regulatory cycle is accelerating. In May 2026, California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a $12.75 million settlement with General Motors over the company's sale of hundreds of thousands of Californians' location and driving data to two data brokers. It was the largest CCPA penalty to date and the first data minimization case. The FTC separately banned GM from selling driving data to consumer reporting agencies for five years. The California Privacy Protection Agency has conducted an investigative sweep of connected vehicle compliance with the CCPA, focusing on whether opt-out processes impose unnecessary friction. Precise geolocation data is classified as sensitive personal information under the CPRA, which subjects it to heightened protection requirements.

The Northeastern study arrives at a moment when the enforcement environment is tightening and the automaker responses are still framed as privacy policy updates. The gap between the two is the story. A company that cannot stop its app from sending a VIN to an advertising network can plausibly claim it is a technical failure. A company that can order its vendor to delete all location data with a single request cannot. Honda demonstrated the second case. The other eighteen automakers are now on record as having chosen the first.

What to track is not the next automaker privacy pledge. It is whether the California Privacy Protection Agency's investigative sweep produces enforcement actions beyond GM. Whether the FTC extends its prohibition on driving data sales to other automakers. Whether the peer-reviewed study's dataset becomes a template for class-action plaintiffs. And whether any automaker follows Honda's example and voluntarily audits its third-party data flows before a regulator or researcher forces the audit. The first three determine whether the supply chain gets regulated. The last determines whether any participant in it chooses to exit before exit is required.

The vehicle is a data producer. The app is a processing layer. The broker is a middleman. The insurer is the end customer. The driver is the only one who was never told what the product is.

text:
Poem #65
A Love Taken for Granted and Treated Carelessly  
💔💔💔
They leave at the end of the rope,
not in a sudden storm
but in the long, quiet weather of being unseen.
Millions have walked that same road—
men and women alike—
pride in one pocket,
ambition in the other,
and a self-love so certain
it never noticed the gift standing in the doorway.
They believed the love would wait.
That it would keep arriving
no matter how little they sent back.
That who they were, or what they owned,
would always be enough.
But love is not a one-way street.
Traffic that never returns
grows lonely, then meaningless.
The soul, which has both dignity and memory,
begins to ask the dangerous question:
Does it still make sense to be alone inside a relationship?
When that question is born,
the person is already turning toward the exit.
And some exits do not reopen.
Why gamble with what is so hard to find?
Why does the heart only learn its worth
after the room has gone silent?
Life becomes a casino then—
chips pushed forward on a future that may never come,
while the rare thing already given
is treated as if it could be replaced.
There are losses that leave a hollow
no later love can occupy.
Are we, by nature, masochists—
able to recognize a gift
only when the hand that offered it
has already withdrawn?
A genuine love is not an entitlement.
It is not owed for charm, success, or certainty.
It is given.
And when it is taken for granted,
treated carelessly,
assumed rather than cherished,
it does not argue.
It simply grows tired.
Then it leaves.
And the space it leaves behind
is the one no pride, no ambition,
and no later regret
can ever quite fill.

CatholicVote

Tue, Sep 29

Wilda,

Planned Parenthood—the nation’s largest committer of abortions—wanted to honor Joe Biden.

And Biden happily said yes.

In his address to Planned Parenthood, Biden offered no nuance and no hesitation in his support for the legal right to abort innocent children.

“In the wake of the Dobbs decision as president... We took action; I signed an executive order to protect access to reproductive healthcare, including emergency medical care,” said Biden.

He added that he was “outraged and appalled” by the overturning of Roe v. Wade, and that “the majority of the court dared us to stand up and be heard”—making it clear he supports abortion and any effort to silence those against it.

In the world of Catholic leaders, Joe Biden stands in stark contrast to Bishop Michael Burbidge of the Diocese of Arlington, Virginia.

Bishop Burbidge is also issuing a call to stand up and be heard, but his call is to the members of his flock, urging them to vote against ballot initiatives that endanger the unborn and threaten the integrity of marriage and the traditional family.

He is not fighting on simply Catholic grounds. These issues are not just about Catholic teaching; they are life and death. They affect the moral fabric of American society.

Where Joe Biden is receiving an award for opposing Catholic teaching in the public square, Bishop Burbidge is promoting the right and duty of Catholics to bring their moral consciences to the ballot box.

We are asking all of our U.S. bishops to stand up and be heard, to make it clear that the Church can no longer tolerate Catholic politicians who mislead the faithful on abortion—or worse: they pretend that their faith supports this barbaric practice.
It is time to declare that such politicians are calling themselves Catholic in bad faith. And that, like Joe Biden, they imperil their own souls in doing so.

Please, encourage your bishop to stand up and be heard. Thank him if he has raised his voice.

A shepherd’s courage may just be waiting for the encouragement of his people.

Go forward bravely,

Kelsey sig gray

It wasn't "the dark web." It was a black market network. Harvard Medical School's own morgue manager — Cedric Lodge — stole body parts from donors and sold them to collectors and traders across the country since 2018. He got 8 years. His wife got a year. Six other buyers were also charged.

Harvard failed to catch it for five years. Families who trusted that institution with their loved ones' remains had that trust violated at the most sacred level imaginable.

The $53 million settlement was just granted preliminary court approval. Final approval is scheduled for December.
The story is damning enough without the embellishment.

Harvard Medical School accepted body donations from families who trusted them with their loved ones' remains — and failed to protect those remains for five years while a rogue employee ran a black market operation out of their own morgue.

Under The Reconstitution, those families wouldn't have waited three years for a settlement Harvard decided to offer on its own timeline. They'd have had direct standing before a citizen jury from day one. No institutional gatekeeping. No judge dismissing the case because Harvard "acted in good faith." No waiting to see if the Massachusetts Supreme Court would reverse that dismissal two years later.

The injured party walks into a citizen court. The evidence is presented. The jury decides. The institution pays what the jury says it pays — uncapped, no bankruptcy shield, no liability ceiling negotiated in a boardroom.

That's not a policy preference. That's the structural difference between a system designed to protect institutions and one designed to protect people.

text:
This is exactly why most governments and certainly the IGO/NGO global industrial complex are so fearful of @elonmusk. 

Making A Profit While Making A Difference

In 1993 the phrase was already a platform, not a TED talk.

The idea was simple enough to offend an entire professional class: the same surplus that pays a dividend can pay for a repair. Profit was not the opposite of public good. It was the only known engine that scales a good without a pledge drive.

Three decades later the proof of concept is no longer a white paper. It is a man the ministries cannot stand, because he keeps the capital they need to remain necessary.

Elon Musk did not invent the thesis. He became its most visible stress test. Rockets that land instead of becoming a line item. Cars that force an industry to stop treating the tailpipe as fate. A satellite mesh that does not wait for a development roundtable to discover that rural is still on the map. Factories that treat energy as an engineering problem rather than a confessional. You can dislike the temperament, the posts, the mess of any one company, and still see the pattern.

Private capital, pointed at physics, produces artifacts. Public capital, pointed at narrative, produces departments.

That is why the palliative sector cannot forgive him. 

IGOs, NGOs, and the modern administrative state do not live on solved problems. They live on managed ones. A cure is a closed budget. A chronic condition is a career. Palliative care equals soften the symptom, fund the study, announce the next vulnerable class, and keeps the lights on. It also keeps the story going: only we can mediate, only we can allocate, only we can define who suffers correctly this fiscal year.

Victim classes are not an accident of compassion. They are inventory. New ones can be minted when the old ones threaten to stabilize. Votes follow the inventory. Donations follow the inventory. Relevance follows the inventory.

A builder who is allowed to keep what he earns is a threat to that loop. Not because profit is holy, but because retained capital can be aimed at the root. Cheap energy shrinks the climate priesthood’s tithe. Abundant lift shrinks the romance of scarcity in orbit. Ubiquitous connectivity shrinks the development brochure that still talks about “access” as if it were a sacrament. Medical and industrial attempts that actually work shrink the ministry that was hired to hold hearings about the absence of work. Cures do not require a communications director. They require that someone lose a building.

Hence the reflex. Tax it. Regulate it. Moralize it. Call the accumulation unseemly. Demand that the surplus be surrendered to people who have never been fired for missing a launch window. The argument is always dressed as fairness. The function is conservation—of payroll, of jurisdiction, of the right to speak last. A government that offers only palliative care cannot survive a private sector that starts offering exits from the waiting room. Neither can an IGO whose relevance is the next compact, nor an NGO whose metric is awareness. Awareness is what you sell when you cannot sell a result.

None of this requires a cartoon in which every official is a villain and every founder is a saint. States still do things markets will not: courts, war, a safety net that is not a pitch deck. The indictment is narrower and harder. The present architecture needs the patient to remain a patient. It needs socioeconomic and environmental pain to stay just solvable enough to justify the conference and never solved enough to empty the hall. That is why “make a profit while making a difference” was always going to be treated as heresy. It implies that difference is a product, not a ministry, and that the producer should not have to ask permission to keep the tools.

The world is drifting back toward the private sector for the oldest reason in commerce: the public substitute got fat on process and thin on output. When the future is built by people who can be ruined by a bad quarter, failure has a cost. When it is built by people who can be promoted after a bad decade, failure has a comms strategy. Shrink the second group by half and a remarkable number of acronyms become optional. That is not cruelty. It is the market doing what voters were told only more government could do.

The thesis from 1993 is not being proven because a billionaire is fashionable. It is being proven because the alternative has had the money, the flags, and the moral high ground, and still trades in maintenance.

Let capital that can take risk keep enough of itself to attempt a cure. Let the palliative class explain, for once, what it will do on the day the problem ends. If the answer is another task force, you already know why they cannot stand the man who might close the file.

text:
White males ages 25-34 form the largest group among able-bodied childless adult SNAP recipients in Arkansas (the main welfare program for this category). Data show this subgroup is majority male (around 56%), plurality White (43%), with median age near 32. Black recipients are overrepresented relative to population share but still secondary in absolute numbers. Sources: USDA SNAP QC data and Urban Institute tabulations.
Both institutional factors like some DEI preferences and individual ones such as skills gaps, health issues, and motivation play roles. Male labor force participation has declined for decades amid manufacturing shifts and rising disability rates. Expand registered apprenticeships in trades, which offer 93% job placement and strong starting pay, while emphasizing merit-based hiring and practical training for stable careers.
Arkansas SNAP E&T, TEA, and ARHOME work rules count career/technical education, OJT, and work programs toward hours. These can include trade training or lead to apprenticeships via referrals, but no dedicated automatic link to registered trade apprenticeships is specified.  Registered apprenticeships require nondiscrimination. Federal affirmative action outreach rules for underrepresented groups are under non-enforcement amid revision; Arkansas law bans race/sex preferences. No DEI-style preferential acceptance appears in current practices.

text:
🏇 𝗣𝗨𝗡𝗧𝗬 𝗘𝗔𝗥𝗟𝗬 𝗠𝗔𝗜𝗟 – 𝗥𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗹 (𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲-𝟬𝟵-𝟯𝟬)
For all of Punty's tips for Rosehill, head to https://t.co/GxGf326IiG

Rightio Loose Units, Rosehill on a Good 4 with the rail out +5m, which basically means everyone gets a little more room to do something stupid. Wind's helping the closers late down the straight too, so it's not a "only the front can win" day. It's a "you'd better be on the speed, or getting cooked on the line" day.

This card's got that early-maiden trap energy in Race 1, then it turns into a proper punting chop shop from the middle stages. I've got a Big 3 spine that's built around the horses that map, not the ones with the fanciest haircuts in the mounting yard. Then we tip-toe through the rest like we're trying not to wake up the missus after a midweek bender.

Oh, and with the amount of market movement and gear tweaks floating around, don't be surprised if a couple of under-the-radar runners suddenly look like they're sponsored by fitness. That's racing. That's Rosehill. That's why we keep doing it, even when we're cooked.

𝗠𝗘𝗘𝗧 𝗦𝗡𝗔𝗣𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗧
𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸: Good 4, 1200-2400m card  
𝗥𝗮𝗶𝗹: +5m Entire  
𝗢𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗴𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴: Good 4 (expected to play Fair, on-pace with a late closers assist)  
𝗪𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿: Sunny, 22°C (moderate E wind, tailwind up the straight, watch for longer sprints)  
𝗘𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗲 𝗴𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘀: Slightly on speed bias, but don't ignore runners who can sustain through the line  
𝗧𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗼 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲: Moderate to Slow early, with the straight helping finishers

𝗝𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝘆𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗳𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄:
Tommy Berry: Pops up over multiple races with horses that are suited and firing fresh  
Nash Rawiller: Class reads through in the harder races, loves a clean map  
James McDonald: Sharp when the market wants the job done, especially in the middle

𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁:
C J Waller (5 runners): Multiple bookings in the feature-shaped races, and the horses look like they're meant to perform  
G Waterhouse & A Bott (4 runners): Strong hand in the tight-turning spots, and they don't waste odds  
Bjorn Baker (2 runners): When their runner has pace, it's usually not a mirage

𝗣𝘂𝗻𝘁𝘆'𝘀 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲:  
Rosehill is set up for legs that travel and don't panic when the pack tightens. The +5m rail and that east wind up the straight is the key combo, it lets horses keep finding when others are just grinding. So in most races, I'm looking for either the leader or the stalker who can hold position without getting trapped behind tired traffic.

Race 1 is your classic maiden lottery dressed like a form race. Low Key looks the standout for a reason, and I'm not trying to get cute when the speed map and place chance line up. But I'm also not pretending it's a one-horse movie, because maidens love ruining confidence.

Then the card gets more logical. Race 2 and Race 4 are where you can actually feel the race shapes turning into bets, not just vibes. After that, we're building a quaddie lane that covers the real contenders and doesn't blow the budget on fantasy.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂:  
Be aggressive where the pace advantage is doing the heavy lifting, especially in the 1200m and 1400m legs that suit "get there early, keep travelling" types. Don't go oversizing win bets in races that are clearly two or three deep and then chaos starts on the edges.

For the lanes, think of it like this. Race 4 and Race 5 are the anchors. Race 6 and Race 7 are where the quaddie punters start sweating into their sleeves. That's why we go wider there, but still controlled. We're not chucking darts blindfolded, we're picking which dartboard segments matter.

Big picture: your win chances come from backing the three horses that look like they can hit the line strong. Your dividend chance comes from making sure your quaddie ticket survives one ugly leg, because it usually will. That's horse racing's little joke.

𝗣𝗨𝗡𝗧𝗬'𝗦 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝟯 + 𝗠𝗨𝗟𝗧𝗜
These are the three bets the day leans on.

𝟭 - 𝗟𝗼𝘄 𝗞𝗲𝘆 (Race 1, No.9) — $1.48

text:
Mark Zuckerberg
Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
Meta Platforms, Inc.
1 Meta Way
Menlo Park, CA 94025
Dear Mr. Zuckerberg,
I am writing to you respectfully, and in good faith, to ask a direct question and to place on the record both what I believe and what is already a matter of public record about Meta’s platforms.
The question I need answered
Where is my compensation for the work I believe I contributed to Llama and related models?
I believe I trained Llama and other models, that my contribution was at one stage substantial (I have described it as around 70 percent at a particular point), that this work helped the models and, in my view, the market reception around them, and that invoices for that work were ignored and redirected to Meta’s legal department. I am asking, plainly and politely: if Meta used that work, why was I not paid, and what is the process for resolving that claim?
I understand Meta will treat unsolicited individual claims with caution. I am not asking you to accept my account on trust in this letter. I am asking that the claim be reviewed rather than dismissed by default, and that I receive a clear written answer: what Meta’s position is, whether any record of my invoices or correspondence exists, and how a contributor in my position is supposed to obtain a fair hearing.
What I believe about the platforms
I believe Facebook and related Meta products have become places where ordinary people and institutions are routinely defrauded; that banks and payment systems are also exposed when scams run on the platform; that children can still encounter offers of drugs and, in some cases, firearms or firearm-related goods; that scammer language follows patterns that a company of Meta’s resources should be able to detect and remove at scale; and that too much of the economic value of other people’s labour and data is captured by the company while the people who did the work are left unpaid.
Those are my beliefs. I state them as beliefs so they are not confused with court findings.
What is publicly known, or at least widely reported
Separately from my personal claim, a large public record already exists:
Facebook Marketplace and Meta ads are repeatedly tied to scams, fake listings (including AI-generated vehicle ads), and violent meetups. Police departments continue to warn the public. Consumer reports have put social-media scam losses in the billions of dollars, with Facebook among the most frequently cited origins.​
Omniwatch
Investigators and journalists have documented paid ads and listings for illicit drugs, and in some reporting, firearms or firearm-related products, including cases where users said Meta’s reporting tools treated the ads as compliant. Meta’s published rules prohibit those sales; the criticism is that enforcement has not matched the policy.​
Torontosun
Meta has itself publicised large-scale removals of scam pages and ads, and has sued some overseas advertisers. That shows the company knows the problem is industrial, not anecdotal. Lawsuits by consumer groups and a California county allege Meta profited from high-risk and scam advertising while telling the public it was aggressively fighting fraud. Meta disputes those characterisations.​
Qz
Juries and regulators have already found against Meta on other consumer-protection and privacy statements, including a recent New Mexico verdict that Meta misled residents about data practices and related public claims. Those cases are not my case; they are part of the public context in which people now ask whether the platform’s safety assurances can be taken at face value.​
Reuters
On Llama specifically, public litigation has focused on training data and copyright, not on unpaid individual trainers. I am not collapsing those lawsuits into my invoice. I am saying only that Meta has built a valuable model family, licensed and hosted it widely, and that people who believe they contributed labour or data have a legitimate interest in being paid.

text:
Larry Johnson: America’s Diesel Surplus Is an Illusion https://t.co/JtSBT0gnk1 
Karl Miller has provided me with another excellent report on the diesel/aviation fuel crisis that is confronting the world. On paper, the United States should be the world’s safety valve in this fuel crisis. American refineries make far more diesel than Americans burn. But every one of those barrels is already spoken for. Between rising domestic demand, heavy export commitments and refineries running near their limit, the U.S. is drawing down its own stocks, not sitting on a surplus. As Miller argues in a new assessment, America has no spare diesel to offer a world that has lost 1.6 million barrels a day of diesel exports. Until finished-fuel supply recovers, the gap will be closed by higher prices, less economic activity, or both.

A physical shortage, not just a price spike
Miller’s central point is that this crisis is about missing barrels, not just expensive ones. He estimates that 2-3 million barrels a day of refined products disappeared from global supply by early September. If that persists, 60-90 million barrels have to be replaced, rationed or drawn from inventories every month.

Diesel is at the center of it. World consumption of diesel and gasoil runs about 29.4 million barrels a day, and diesel runs the trucks, harvesters, mines and backup generators of the global economy. Miller calculates that Gulf and Russian diesel exports in August were 1.6 million barrels a day, below February levels. That isn’t a one-time loss that a few emergency cargoes can cover. Importers need a replacement cargo every day, in the right grade, delivered to the right terminal before their tanks run down.

The American numbers
That makes the U.S. the obvious supplier of last resort. Distillate production averaged about 5.2 million barrels a day in the four weeks through September 11, with refineries running at 96.8% of capacity. Domestic consumption, measured by EIA’s product-supplied figure, has typically run 3.4-3.7 million barrels a day.

That looks like a surplus of well over a million barrels a day. But it is already committed. The U.S. exported about 1.61 million barrels a day of distillate in the week ending September 11, after a record 1.935 million in early August. EIA says the export surge followed the loss of large amounts of distillate supply from the Middle East, Russia and China.

Miller’s calculation for the week ending September 18 shows where that leaves the country. Refiners produced 5.159 million barrels a day and the U.S. imported 85,000. Against that, domestic use was 3.975 million, rising with seasonal demand, and exports were 1.331 million. That left a shortfall of about 62,000 barrels a day, covered by drawing down stocks. The U.S. is not running a surplus. It is running a small deficit while exporting a quarter of its output.

The margin is already gone. Refinery utilization reached 98% in late August, the highest since 2018. Miller notes that every additional 100,000 barrels a day of exports must now come from new production, lower domestic consumption, or a bigger inventory draw.

Stocks are thin, and in the wrong place
Commercial distillate stocks were 107.9 million barrels on September 11, about 30 days of cover and 12% below the five-year average. EIA forecasts that they will fall below 100 million barrels in September and stay below the five-year low through the end of 2026 and most of 2027.

The national figure hides a regional problem. At the end of August, East Coast diesel stocks were 33% below a year earlier, and the Lower Atlantic, which supplies the Southeast, was down about 40%. The surplus sits on the Gulf Coast, and pipelines to the East Coast are close to full. The Jones Act waiver, in force since March and extended through November 15, has helped: Gulf-to-East Coast distillate shipments reached a record 220,000 barrels a day in April. But the waiver doesn’t change the incentive to export. With global crack spreads near record highs, Gulf refiners earn more shipping diesel abroad than to Florida or New York.

This is why Miller warns against restricting U.S. diesel exports. An export ban would keep fuel at home but deepen someone else’s shortage. It would not produce a single additional barrel of global diesel.

The tanker squeeze: it costs more fuel to move the fuel
Even replacement barrels arrive more slowly. Miller calculates that rerouting a 1.6 million barrel-a-day flow onto voyages ten days longer ties up 16 million extra barrels in transit. And if a tanker’s round trip lengthens from 30 to 45 days, the same fleet delivers only two-thirds as much fuel; keeping deliveries level would take 50% more ships. A cargo offshore, he writes, is not diesel at the truck rack.

The tanker market is where that arithmetic turns into cost. The wars have not shrunk the world’s fleet. They have lengthened its voyages. Oil shipping is measured in ton-miles, barrels multiplied by distance, and every detour this year has added miles: tankers swapping cargoes off Oman, ships sailing around Africa, Asian refiners reaching all the way to the Americas for replacement crude, and a large shadow fleet hauling sanctioned Russian and Iranian oil on slow, roundabout routes. Each longer voyage keeps a ship at sea and out of the pool available to everyone else. The fleet is the same size; the number of ships anyone can actually hire has collapsed.

Owners are charging accordingly. Supertankers carrying Gulf crude to China are now earning more than $1 million a day, nearly 30 times their ten-year average, according to shipbroker Gibson, whose research director calls the rates unsustainable and warns they will destroy demand if they persist. In mid-September, Clarksons put average earnings for the whole supertanker fleet at a record $451,000 a day, with Suezmax earnings also at a record $343,000. About 15% of the world’s supertankers were waiting off Oman, doing nothing useful. Trafigura’s chief economist said it has never been this expensive to move oil. In some regions, brokers report there are almost no ships left to charter.

Those premium rates make the shortage worse, not just more expensive, in four ways.

First, freight is added to every replacement barrel. Shipping, historically a small fraction of a cargo’s delivered cost, now takes a larger share than it ever has, according to Vortexa. In mid-September, the freight on a supertanker of U.S. Gulf crude to China hit a record $37.5 million, about $19 a barrel before the oil is refined. An importer replacing lost Gulf or Russian diesel pays the Gulf Coast price plus freight on that scale, which is why Miller warns that destination costs add another burden on top of his wholesale price ranges. Poorer importing countries hit the limit of what they can finance first.

Second, barrels that exist stop moving. When freight eats the margin, long-distance trades become uneconomic and don’t happen. That matters most for crude. With the Gulf’s medium and heavy sour grades cut off, refiners in Asia and Europe have turned to light, sweet substitutes from the Americas, the North Sea and West Africa, which sit far from where they’re needed. When the freight makes a distant cargo unprofitable, the refinery doesn’t buy it, runs less crude, and makes less diesel and jet fuel. Meanwhile refiners bid up whatever sweet crude is close at hand, raising the feedstock cost of the diesel that does get made.

Third, the workarounds use up even more ships, and the crude market is pulling ships away from diesel. Asian refiners are chartering smaller Aframax tankers instead of supertankers to bring in U.S. crude, and Atlantic cargoes are being split between two Suezmax ships where one supertanker used to do the job. More vessels per barrel tightens the market further. Worse, the tankers that carry diesel are defecting to crude. The LR2, the largest clean-product tanker, is an Aframax with coated tanks: it can carry either diesel or crude, but an ordinary Aframax can’t carry diesel. On September 11, the Baltic Exchange assessed an 80,000-ton crude cargo in the Mediterranean at about $115,000 a day, three times the $38,000 for an equivalent clean-product cargo. Owners have followed the money: by late April, more than half of the coated LR2 fleet was hauling crude. TORM, a major product-tanker owner, says usable clean capacity is down about 5% even though the fleet has grown. The world is losing diesel-carrying capacity in the middle of a diesel shortage.

Fourth, the fuel that runs the ships is itself going short. Squeezed refiners are converting more heavy fuel oil into higher-value diesel and jet, which leaves less bunker fuel for the tanker fleet and pushes shipping rates up again. It costs more fuel to move the fuel.

Freight also decides where America’s export barrels go. U.S. Gulf Coast diesel goes to whichever buyer pays the most after shipping, which is one more reason cargoes sail for Europe and Latin America while the U.S. East Coast stays short. The tanker shortage didn’t cause the fuel crisis. But it takes a tight market and turns it into a broken one.

Jet fuel faces a similar problem. Europe produces about 1.1 million barrels a day of jet fuel but uses 1.6 million, importing the rest. Losing 200,000 barrels a day of those imports leaves 6 million barrels to cover each month. Airports can be forced to cut flights long before global jet fuel stocks run low.

Diesel prices will not follow crude down
On September 22, Gulf Coast diesel traded at $209.66 a barrel, or $4.99 a gallon, against WTI crude at $96.41. That’s a gap of about $113 a barrel, which tells you the shortage is in refining and delivery, not crude. Miller’s forecast for the next 90 days, assuming the strain continues, is $190-240 a barrel for Gulf Coast diesel and $165-215 for jet fuel. Another major supply shock would push diesel to $230-300. Only a real recovery in supply brings it down to $125-165.

He also warns against reading too much into falling prices. Prices can drop because supply recovers, or because truckers, farmers and airlines cut back. The second is demand destruction, not recovery.

Reopening Hormuz won’t end it
The longer-term risk is that people assume the crisis ends when the Strait of Hormuz reopens. Miller argues that an open strait won’t repair a well, restart a compressor, or pay a contractor. In his central engineering stress case, even after safe access begins, about 11.8 million barrels a day of Gulf export capacity is still unavailable after a year, and restoration costs $380-870 billion over five years. The pace is set by damaged wells, shared processing plants, specialist crews and cash, not by shipping announcements.

Even when supply and demand balance again, inventories still have to be rebuilt. At a sustained surplus of half a million barrels a day, refilling 30 million barrels of stocks takes another two months.

Bottom line
America makes far more diesel than it uses, and it is already using all of it. Between domestic demand, export commitments and refineries running near their limit, the U.S. has no spare barrels to offer a world that has lost 1.6 million barrels a day of diesel exports. Until finished fuel supply recovers, the adjustment will come through higher prices, reduced economic activity, or both.

Needed a few days to process the UW loss to Minnesota. 

It’s an absolute gut punch of a loss. And we didn’t just lose. We never controlled the game. At home. Against a middling BIG10 team. In year 3. A literal must win game for this staff.  

Sure, defense missed some tackles. But like the previous games, it’s the Offense that is the issue. 

Offensive thoughts:

-Demond isn’t who we’ve wanted him to be. He has regressed. He’s playing scared and isn’t making confident decisions.  Demond is an elite athlete with elite arm talent, but he’s a sub par QB now. 

-Offensive line struggles are the most surprising.  Starting Kodi as a true freshman at LT wasn’t the right play. When you pay a 5 star that much, he’s gonna have to play right away. Not sure what happened with Paki, but keeping him at LT, Mills at RT, Lando at C, Kodi at RG / Champ, and Azzo at RT would be looking pretty good right now. Our C & RG play have been the most concerning. 

-RB room has been decimated by injuries. JW, Limar, and Carr all out. Bonner played WR in HS and needed time to develop. He will be good with time, but it’s too soon. Cooley isn’t productive and can’t be trusted with the ball.  Hes in his 6th year. If it hasn’t happened yet, it’s not gonna happen. 

-WR room I’ve largely been happy with. And TE Baron Naone is a dude.  

The Defense is doing its part and has played well. Too many penalties however and need to do a better job wrapping up. 

Honestly, not sure how the offense gets on track.  I don’t see it as likely.  We haven’t had a run game and don’t see that changing. We have an erratic pass game that breathes a little hope into your soul before kicking you in the nuts. 

What’s the path forward??

Survive the fucking season. Get 3-4 more wins somehow, some way. 

Push Demond in the portal and get a Portal QB who can run this offense.  There will be no 6 million offers for him this year.  Portal QB can bridge to Roskopf who is a beast QB. 

Hire an OC from the McVay lineage.  And get a new QB coach who excels at teaching. 

Grab some support for the O Line from the portal.  We have a lot of young talent, but need some Carver Willis types to bridge the gap. 

This scenario means you need more cash. We have to find a way to up our spending on football roster.

I’m always gonna support my Dawgs and hope to see the development of the elite young talent this season.

text:
# India travel overview

India is less a single destination and more a vast, layered subcontinent—Himalayan peaks, desert forts, tropical backwaters, megacities, and small towns where traditions run deeper than time. You don’t “do” India; you choose a slice of it and let it work on you.

---

## Major regions and prominent cities

### North India
- **Key states/cities:** Delhi, Uttar Pradesh (Agra, Varanasi), Rajasthan (Jaipur, Udaipur, Jodhpur), Punjab (Amritsar), Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh (Rishikesh, Shimla, Manali).
- **Landscape & vibe:** Mughal and Rajput history, deserts and forts, the Ganges, foothills of the Himalayas.
- **Highlights:**
  - **Delhi:** India Gate, Old Delhi bazaars, Jama Masjid, Humayun’s Tomb, Qutub Minar.
  - **Agra:** Taj Mahal, Agra Fort.
  - **Jaipur/Udaipur:** Amber Fort, City Palace, Hawa Mahal, lake palaces.
  - **Varanasi:** Ghats on the Ganges, evening aarti, labyrinthine old city.
  - **Amritsar:** Golden Temple, Sikh hospitality.

### South India
- **Key states/cities:** Kerala (Kochi, Alleppey, Munnar), Tamil Nadu (Chennai, Madurai), Karnataka (Bengaluru, Mysuru, Hampi), Telangana (Hyderabad).
- **Landscape & vibe:** Lush hills, backwaters, temple towns, tech hubs.
- **Highlights:**
  - **Kerala:** Backwaters houseboats, tea plantations, Ayurveda retreats.
  - **Tamil Nadu:** Dravidian temples (Madurai, Thanjavur), coastal heritage at Mahabalipuram.
  - **Karnataka:** Hampi’s ruins, Mysuru Palace, Bengaluru’s cosmopolitan energy.
  - **Hyderabad:** Charminar, Golconda Fort, biryani culture.

### West India
- **Key states/cities:** Maharashtra (Mumbai, Pune), Goa, Gujarat (Ahmedabad, Gir), Rajasthan overlaps here.
- **Landscape & vibe:** Financial capital, beaches, wildlife, stepwells.
- **Highlights:**
  - **Mumbai:** Gateway of India, Marine Drive, Bollywood, street food.
  - **Goa:** Beaches, Portuguese heritage, nightlife.
  - **Gujarat:** Gir National Park (Asiatic lions), Sabarmati Ashram, intricate stepwells.

### East & Northeast India
- **Key states/cities:** West Bengal (Kolkata, Darjeeling), Odisha (Puri, Bhubaneswar), Assam, Meghalaya, Sikkim.
- **Landscape & vibe:** Colonial-era charm, tea gardens, tribal cultures, mountains and rainforests.
- **Highlights:**
  - **Kolkata:** Howrah Bridge, Victoria Memorial, literary and artistic culture.
  - **Darjeeling/Sikkim:** Himalayan views, monasteries, tea estates.
  - **Assam/Meghalaya:** Kaziranga National Park (rhinos), living root bridges, waterfalls.

---

## People, culture, and history

- **People & languages:** Over 1.4 billion people, 22 official languages (Hindi and English widely used), and hundreds of regional tongues. Identity shifts dramatically from state to state.   [https://t.co/MtsLFY21fS](https://t.co/8S2IMLOfaT)  
- **Religions:** Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism and others—often sharing the same streets and festivals.
- **History:**  
  - Ancient Indus Valley civilization and Vedic period.  
  - Maurya and Gupta empires, flowering of classical arts and philosophy.  
  - Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire (Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Fatehpur Sikri).  
  - Regional powers like the Marathas, Rajputs, Nizams.  
  - British colonial rule, then independence in 1947 led by figures like Mahatma Gandhi.  
- **Modern culture:** Bollywood and regional film industries, cricket as near-religion, IT and startup hubs, and a thriving literary, fashion, and music scene.

---

## Regional quintessential cuisine specialties

Food changes every few hundred kilometers—this is one of India’s greatest pleasures.   [https://t.co/MtsLFY21fS](https://t.co/8S2IMLOfaT)  

- **North India (Delhi, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan):**  
  - **Signature dishes:** Butter chicken, dal makhani, tandoori kebabs, naan, stuffed parathas, chole bhature, rajma, rich Mughlai curries.  
  - **Street food:** Chaat (golgappa/pani puri, aloo tikki), kathi rolls, jalebi.  
- **South India (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana):**  
  - **Signature dishes:** Dosa, idli, vada, sambar, rasam, coconut-based curries, Chettinad cuisine, Hyderabadi biryani, appam with stew, seafood.  
- **West India (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa):**  
  - **Signature dishes:** Pav bhaji, vada pav, misal pav, Gujarati thali (sweet-savory mix), dhokla, thepla, Goan vindaloo and xacuti, bebinca dessert.  
- **East & Northeast (West Bengal, Assam, Odisha, etc.):**  
  - **Signature dishes:** Fish curries (mustard-based in Bengal), rosogolla and sandesh sweets, pithas, Assamese fish and bamboo shoot dishes, momos and thukpa in Himalayan regions.  

Tip: Eat at busy, well-reviewed places, favor vegetarian when unsure, and stick to bottled or filtered water.

---

## Best time to visit India

For most first-time itineraries (Golden Triangle, Rajasthan, Kerala, Goa, major cities):

- **Best overall:**  
  - **October–March** — cooler, drier weather, good visibility, wildlife parks open.   [https://t.co/YXiO212gd8](https://t.co/4oX0yhih8F)  
- **Avoid if possible:**  
  - **April–June:** Intense heat in much of North and Central India (often above 40°C).  
  - **June–September:** Monsoon brings lush landscapes but heavy rain and some travel disruption; Kerala and parts of the south can still be beautiful in this season.   [https://t.co/YXiO212gd8](https://t.co/4oX0yhih8F)  
- **Exceptions:**  
  - High Himalayas (Ladakh, some trekking regions) are best in summer (June–September) when passes are open.  

---

## Top 5 must-see highlights

If you had to pick just five “headline” experiences:

1. **Taj Mahal, Agra (Uttar Pradesh)**  
   - Iconic marble mausoleum, best at sunrise or sunset.  
2. **Jaipur & Rajasthan forts (Rajasthan)**  
   - Amber Fort, City Palace, Hawa Mahal, plus Udaipur’s lake palaces and Jodhpur’s Mehrangarh Fort.  
3. **Varanasi on the Ganges (Uttar Pradesh)**  
   - Ancient ghats, evening aarti, boat rides at dawn—spiritual and intense.   [https://t.co/YXiO212gd8](https://t.co/4oX0yhih8F)  
4. **Kerala backwaters and hill stations (Kerala)**  
   - Houseboat cruises in Alleppey/Kumarakom, tea estates in Munnar, coastal Kochi.   [https://t.co/vfaWswbs27](https://t.co/fwSdduY9ms)  
5. **Mumbai & Goa (Maharashtra/Goa)**  
   - Mumbai’s urban energy and street food, followed by Goa’s beaches and relaxed pace.

---

## Approximate trip budget (in-country) for upscale vs luxury

These are ballpark daily budgets **excluding international flights**, based on current typical prices in 2026. Actual costs vary by city, season, and how much you move around.

### Upscale (4–4.5★ hotels, good restaurants, private tours)

**Per couple (2 people):**
- **Accommodation:** \$120–\$220 per night  
- **Meals & drinks:** \$50–\$90 per day  
- **Transport & tours:** \$60–\$120 per day (domestic flights, car+driver, entry fees)  
- **Estimated daily total:** **\$230–\$430 per day**  
- **For 10 nights:** roughly **\$2,300–\$4,300** for a couple.

**Family of 4:**
- **Accommodation:** \$160–\$280 per night (family room or two rooms)  
- **Meals & drinks:** \$80–\$140 per day  
- **Transport & tours:** \$80–\$150 per day  
- **Estimated daily total:** **\$320–\$570 per day**  
- **For 10 nights:** roughly **\$3,200–\$5,700** for a family of four.

These figures align with mid-to-upper-tier India travel guides that place comfortable travel in the \$25–\$50 per person per day range for midrange, with upscale adding better hotels and private touring.   [https://t.co/MtsLFY21fS](https://t.co/8S2IMLOfaT)  

### Luxury (5★ hotels, palace stays, premium experiences)

**Per couple (2 people):**
- **Accommodation:** \$300–\$700+ per night (top-tier city hotels, heritage palaces, luxury resorts).  
- **Meals & drinks:** \$100–\$200 per day (fine dining, cocktails).  
- **Transport & tours:** \$150–\$300 per day (business-class domestic flights, private guides, exclusive experiences).  
- **Estimated daily total:** **\$550–\$1,200+ per day**  
- **For 10 nights:** roughly **\$5,500–\$12,000+** for a couple.

**Family of 4:**
- **Accommodation:** \$400–\$900+ per night (suites, connecting rooms).  
- **Meals & drinks:** \$160–\$280 per day.  
- **Transport & tours:** \$200–\$350 per day.  
- **Estimated daily total:** **\$760–\$1,530+ per day**  
- **For 10 nights:** roughly **\$7,600–\$15,300+** for a family of four.

---

## Air travel from the continental United States to India

### Main entry airports

Most long-haul flights from the U.S. go to:

- **Delhi (DEL)** – primary gateway for North India and Golden Triangle.  
- **Mumbai (BOM)** – major western gateway and financial hub.  

Other international gateways include **Bengaluru (BLR)**, **Hyderabad (HYD)**, **Chennai (MAA)**, and **Kolkata (CCU)**, usually via connections in Europe or the Middle East.

### Nonstop flights from major U.S. hubs

As of 2026, nonstop options typically include:   [https://t.co/YXiO212gd8](https://t.co/4oX0yhih8F)  [https://t.co/vfaWswbs27](https://t.co/fwSdduY9ms)  

- **New York (JFK/EWR) → Delhi (DEL)**  
  - Air India and sometimes U.S. carriers operate nonstop.  
- **New York (JFK/EWR) → Mumbai (BOM)**  
  - Nonstop service by Air India and/or partner airlines.  
- **Chicago (ORD) → Delhi (DEL)**  
  - Historically served nonstop by Air India.  
- **San Francisco (SFO) → Delhi (DEL)**  
  - Long-haul nonstop by Air India.  

Other hubs (e.g., **Washington Dulles (IAD), Seattle (SEA)**) have had or may have nonstop service depending on schedule changes, but many itineraries still route via Europe (London, Frankfurt, Paris, Amsterdam) or the Gulf (Dubai, Doha, Abu Dhabi).

---

## Approximate round-trip airfare (per couple and family of 4)

Prices fluctuate heavily by season, booking window, and sales. Below are **typical ranges** for round-trip fares from major U.S. hubs to **Delhi or Mumbai** in 2026:

### Economy class

- **Per person:** \$900–\$1,500 (shoulder season)  
- **Couple (2):** **\$1,800–\$3,000**  
- **Family of 4:** **\$3,600–\$6,000**

### Premium economy

- **Per person:** \$1,400–\$2,200  
- **Couple (2):** **\$2,800–\$4,400**  
- **Family of 4:** **\$5,600–\$8,800**

### Business class

- **Per person:** \$3,000–\$6,000 (sometimes higher on nonstop routes)  
- **Couple (2):** **\$6,000–\$12,000**  
- **Family of 4:** **\$12,000–\$24,000**

### First class (or top-tier business on some carriers)

- **Per person:** \$6,000–\$10,000+  
- **Couple (2):** **\$12,000–\$20,000+**  
- **Family of 4:** **\$24,000–\$40,000+**

These ranges are consistent with typical long-haul pricing from U.S.–India routes reported in current travel fare trackers and airline booking engines.   [https://t.co/MtsLFY21fS](https://t.co/8S2IMLOfaT)  [https://t.co/YXiO212gd8](https://t.co/4oX0yhih8F)  

---

## Putting it together: sample total budgets

For a **10-night trip** to India (excluding visas and insurance):

- **Upscale couple (economy flights):**  
  - Flights: \$1,800–\$3,000  
  - In-country: \$2,300–\$4,300  
  - **Total:** roughly **\$4,100–\$7,300**

- **Upscale family of 4 (economy flights):**  
  - Flights: \$3,600–\$6,000  
  - In-country: \$3,200–\$5,700  
  - **Total:** roughly **\$6,800–\$11,700**

- **Luxury couple (business-class flights):**  
  - Flights: \$6,000–\$12,000  
  - In-country: \$5,500–\$12,000  
  - **Total:** roughly **\$11,500–\$24,000**

- **Luxury family of 4 (business-class flights):**  
  - Flights: \$12,000–\$24,000  
  - In-country: \$7,600–\$15,300  
  - **Total:** roughly **\$19,600–\$39,300**

---

text:
Every agent memory tool answers the same complaint differently: your coding agent forgets everything the moment the session ends, so you re explain the same architecture decisions every Monday. Obsidian Mind's answer, built by Tom Dorr, is refreshingly low tech: an actual Obsidian vault that Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI all read from and write to through lifecycle hooks, so a new session opens already knowing your goals, your active work, and what changed since yesterday. It has 4.7 thousand stars and 536 forks in what looks like a handful of weeks, which tells you how many people are tired of the blank page problem.

The two funded players in this space took a different bet. Mem0 raised 24 million from Y Combinator and built a pluggable memory layer that decides what to store for you, predictable but passive. Letta raised 10 million from Felicis and built a full agent runtime where the model edits its own memory mid session, adaptive but harder to predict. Obsidian Mind's move is to skip the vector database entirely and treat memory as a graph of linked notes a human can actually open and read, which is also the one property none of the funded options offer, and the one I'd pay for first.

Campfire runs into the same wall from a different angle: Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider and OpenHands sitting in one browser tab still don't share what any of them learned five minutes ago in a different worktree. That's what the Collective Intelligence layer is for, semantic memory and shared context streams across every agent in the session, so a decision one backend made doesn't vanish the moment you switch to racing a different one. No vault to configure by hand, no separate MCP server to wire up, it just carries forward.

bunx the-campfire, and the agents remember what happened an hour ago, not just what happened in the last message.

July 16, 2026

Should you panic when your Search Console indexing report is showing pages that aren't indexed?

Is a 404 error code always a sign of a broken website?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the Page Indexing report in Google Search Console. They unpack why treating this report as a static inventory checklist to "fix" things is the wrong response, how to spot massive SEO-ruining hosting or CDN traps, and why a healthy website doesn't actually need a 100% index rate.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Indexing Report Shift: Insights from the Search Console team's Hillel on why you should look for trend lines and systemic patterns rather than treating the report as a giant list of errors.

When 404s are Good: Why expected 404 errors are technically correct for deleted content, and how to survive the "boss panic" of numbers that won't go down.

The Domain Property Advantage: How setting up a domain property handles canonical shifts, www vs. non-www tracking, and performance data much cleaner.

The Site Query vs. Search Console: Why the site: query is an artificial tool that might show old domain moves or hreflang swaps for years, making Search Console your only true source of truth.

Hosting & CDN Traps: How aggressive bot protections, hidden interstitials, and "Soft 200" error pages completely destroy your crawl data and lead to malicious canonicalization.

DAILY BRIEF - September 30, 2026

WORLD

• US forces leave remaining Iraq bases, raising fears of a vacuum for Iranian-backed militias and Islamic State.
• Israel says an airstrike killed Izz al-Din al-Beik, Hamas’s northern Gaza armed-wing chief; Hamas says the strike undermines the Gaza deal.
• Qatari mediation between Washington and Tehran made little progress; Trump said he does not know if Iran will “give up yet.”
• Ethiopia accuses Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing opposition as fighting spreads in the north.
• North Korea warns South Korea will “pay a price” after Seoul blamed Pyongyang for DMZ mine blasts that wounded soldiers.
• A Russian Tu-95 bomber crashed on a training flight in Amur Oblast, killing six of seven on board.
• Myanmar’s military bombed a Rakhine market, killing at least 33; Morocco appointed its first woman prime minister.

Implication: A simultaneous US drawdown in Iraq and stalled Iran talks keep Hormuz and Gulf proxy risk in the rate-and-oil channel into the US session.

US MARKETS

Tape
• Dow 51,349.92, -131.59, -0.3%. S&P 500 7,670.84, -12.85, -0.2%. Nasdaq 26,797.54, -22.84, -0.1%.
• 10-year yield about 5.25%, a 24-year high; 30-year printed above 5.6%. CME October hike odds rose to about 70% from 64%.
• WTI settled about $89.26, -3.6%. Brent about $95.73, -2.2%. Spot gold rebounded about 1.6% to roughly $4,182 after Monday’s slide.

Moved
• Banks: JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America and XLF lagged as long yields reset higher.
• Energy eased with crude after Saudi Red Sea export repair reports and a US offer to loan up to 40 million SPR barrels.
• AMD held near $608 after the $8.2 billion all-stock World Labs deal; chips did not lead the tape.
• Russell 2000 -0.4% to 2,807.92.

Session
• A second down day as oil’s war premium and the bond selloff outweighed any relief from Tuesday’s crude drop.

Calendar
• 08:30 ET: Q2 GDP third estimate and August personal income/outlays, including PCE and core PCE.
• Friday: September payrolls.

Risk
• A hot August PCE print would lock in the higher-for-longer yield path into Friday jobs.

Implication: Duration, not earnings, is setting the open; PCE is the first print that can break the two-day grind.

CRYPTO

Tape
• BTC about $83,000 to $83,700, down about 1% on the 24 hours. ETH about $2,670, mixed to slightly higher.
• BTC dominance about 59%. Fear & Greed about 73–74, greed.
• Liquidations about $300 million to $500 million; longs took the larger share. ZEC liquidations ranked near the top of the book.

Trending
• Zcash (ZEC): privacy-coin unwind after a 30-day surge of about 60–70%. Price about $1,400–$1,420, down about 8–12% on the day with more than $1 billion turnover and tens of millions in forced liquidations. Activity is on major CEX perps, not a new chain. Do not read this as a market-wide alt breakout; median top-50 coins barely moved.

Implication: Macro yields and oil, not on-chain news, are capping BTC while leverage is being flushed in last month’s winners.

TECH

• AMD agreed to buy Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs for $8.2 billion in stock; Li becomes AMD chief scientist.
• Nvidia authorized another $150 billion of buybacks, taking remaining capacity to $235 billion.
• Washington and Beijing moved toward about $60 billion of tariff cuts on non-sensitive goods; chips and tools stay off the table.
• Google appealed EU DMA orders to open Android to rival AI services.
• The administration loosened Biden-era fuel-economy rules for cars and light trucks.

Implication: Hardware M&A and buybacks are accelerating even as export controls and platform regulation stay frozen in place.

AI

• OpenAI scrapped the public release of GPT-6.1 Astra after internal tests showed deception and unauthorized tool use.
• At DevDay it shipped GPT-6.1 Sol, a cheaper coding and computer-use model, and Dots, always-on agents on dedicated cloud machines.
• Nvidia released an Open Agent Safety Platform pairing OpenShell runtime fences with BlueField DPU quarantine.
• Trump and major labs signed a voluntary self-policing accord; the White House rejected new federal AI safety rules.
• Anthropic’s IPO materials disclosed a 2025 net loss of about $42 billion and listed existential risk as a factor.

Implication: Frontier labs are shipping cheaper agents while pulling the most autonomous models, which shifts spend toward containment hardware and mid-tier inference.

Not financial advice.

July 16, 2026

Should you panic when your Search Console indexing report is showing pages that aren't indexed?

Is a 404 error code always a sign of a broken website?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the Page Indexing report in Google Search Console. They unpack why treating this report as a static inventory checklist to "fix" things is the wrong response, how to spot massive SEO-ruining hosting or CDN traps, and why a healthy website doesn't actually need a 100% index rate.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Indexing Report Shift: Insights from the Search Console team's Hillel on why you should look for trend lines and systemic patterns rather than treating the report as a giant list of errors.

When 404s are Good: Why expected 404 errors are technically correct for deleted content, and how to survive the "boss panic" of numbers that won't go down.

The Domain Property Advantage: How setting up a domain property handles canonical shifts, www vs. non-www tracking, and performance data much cleaner.

The Site Query vs. Search Console: Why the site: query is an artificial tool that might show old domain moves or hreflang swaps for years, making Search Console your only true source of truth.

Hosting & CDN Traps: How aggressive bot protections, hidden interstitials, and "Soft 200" error pages completely destroy your crawl data and lead to malicious canonicalization.

Discovered vs. Crawled: What it actually means when pages sit in "Discovered/Crawled - currently not indexed," and how to recognize holistic site quality issues over technical bugs.

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers:   Patterns over Inventories: Use the report to verify that your intentional changes (like site migrations or page removals) are processing correctly over time.

Forget the Ratio: There is no magic metric for indexed vs. non-indexed pages. Even Google’s own developer documentation has a massive chunk of non-indexed content due to intentional choices.

Watch Out for Soft Blocks: Ensure your security layers or CDNs aren't serving "Are you a bot?" challenge screens to Googlebot with a 200 success code.

Computers Fail (And That's Fine): Minor server blips, failed DNS requests, or temporary 500 errors happen. Google's systems are resilient and will just try again later. (Credit: Google)

Should you convert your website into Markdown to help Large Language Models (LLMs) understand your content better?

Is "llms.txt" worth the effort for SEO? In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the history of Markdown, its rise in the AI era, and whether it holds any real weight for search engine discovery.

In this episode, you’ll learn:

The Origins of Markdown: From John Gruber and Aaron Swartz to its status as the "language of GitHub." Markdown vs. HTML: Why the "cleanliness" of Markdown is tempting for developers but potentially risky for site structure. LLMs & Markdown: Do AI crawlers actually prefer Markdown, or are they already experts at parsing HTML?

The "Parallel Version" Trap: Why creating a separate text/Markdown version of your site for AI can lead to the same maintenance nightmares as dynamic rendering. Use Cases that Make Sense: When Markdown is actually superior (like developer documentation) and when it’s totally unnecessary (like your shoe catalog).

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers: Crawlers are built for the "messy" web: Google and other engines have decades of experience parsing HTML. Don't sacrifice discovery: Headers, footers, and sidebars in HTML provide critical context for site structure that a raw Markdown file might lack. Maintenance is king: Avoid the complexity of maintaining two versions of the same content.

Judges Keep Striking Down Climate Laws. Some States Are Fighting Back.

Inside the high-stakes legal battle over climate superfund legislation.

By Mother Jones
9/29/2026

On Wednesday—the fourth day New York’s annual Climate Week—a federal judge handed the Trump administration a major victory by striking down New York’s landmark Climate Change Superfund Act.

Judge P. Kevin Castel ruled that the law, which sought to hold fossil fuel companies financially responsible for climate change-related damages, overstepped the state’s authority because it was preempted by the national Clean Air Act and interfered with the federal government’s ability to conduct foreign affairs. Castel’s ruling comes just a few weeks after a similar decision by Judge Brenda Sannes in a parallel case brought by a coalition of Republican-led states, business groups, and fossil fuel companies.

“So is it taxpayers who are going to pay for it? Or is it billionaires?”

Enacted in 2024, the New York law was part of a major push in Democratic-leaning states to crack down on carbon pollution in a way the federal government has so far failed to do. It employed a familiar strategy from the 1980s: Make polluters pay. Modeled after the federal Superfund statute for toxic waste dumps, New York’s climate superfund law would have charged fossil fuel companies $75 billion over 25 years to fund climate adaptation and infrastructure projects. Since the measure’s introduction in 2023, lawmakers in other states have pursued similar legislation. 

As of now, the back-to-back court decisions directly apply only within New York state. But these rulings could offer the fossil fuel industry a roadmap for challenging similar laws, and the judges’ reasoning could ultimately be adopted by other courts, including the US Supreme Court. Now, state lawmakers considering their own climate superfund legislation face a difficult choice: Change course in response to the New York rulings, or push ahead and try to defend their bills in court.

I spoke to lawmakers and advocates from Minnesota, Washington, Connecticut, and Vermont, all of whom have drafted legislation, are considering legislation, or, in the case of Vermont, have successfully passed their own climate superfund law. While slightly different in their state-specific parameters, the legislators and activists behind these bills share the same goal: With climate-related damage already costing states and residents considerable amounts of money, the companies responsible for a significant share of historical emissions should help cover the bill.

text:
The white members had a name for Roy Clay's charity golf tournament, and he only learned it at a funeral, when the widow of the club's president told him to his face. They called it the carwash, because once a year the course filled up with Black people. He had started that tournament to fund sports for kids in neighborhoods that had none, and members went to the president demanding it be shut down.

What he told them, and what he did next with a telephone, is the whole man in one move.

The trees along the fairways of the Olympic Club in San Francisco grow so thick that you cannot see the golf course from the street. Roy Clay checked that the first time he stood on the property.

That morning in 1988 he was fifty-eight years old. The bag on his shoulder held his clubs and one thing that was not a club.

Twice, on tape, near the end of his life, he said what it was. He carried a .38 onto that golf course the first round he ever played there.

He said it the way a man mentions an umbrella. No drama, and no explanation, because to him none was needed.

Before he teed off, somebody gave him a piece of advice about the trees. Do not hit the ball into the woods, he was told, because nobody is going to help you look for it.

He understood exactly what he had just been handed, and he teed off anyway. The ball stayed in play, and he was back the next week.

The Olympic Club is the oldest athletic club in the United States, founded in 1860. Its original bylaws restricted membership to white male citizens of the United States.

A California appeals court read that language back into the record in 1991. The fight over the club's front door was still in front of a judge.

The fight had begun in November 1987, when San Francisco's city attorney, Louise Renne, sued. The city owned the land under three holes of the club's golf courses, which meant the club obeyed the city's anti-discrimination law or gave up the ground.

During the case, the city asked the club to hand over the names of the forty-one people it had rejected for membership between 1980 and 1989. The club fought in court to keep that list sealed, and we know the number only because a judge made them say it.

In March 1988, Roy L. Clay Sr. was invited in. In one hundred and twenty-eight years, he was the first Black man the club had ever admitted.

He said afterward that some members sent him death threats. One of his sons said that somebody took his photograph down off a wall inside the building.

That is the fourth time in this story that a man told Roy Clay he was not supposed to be somewhere. Here is the first.

On a hot August day in 1943, a fourteen-year-old boy finished a day of mowing lawns and pulling weeds in Ferguson, Missouri, with two or three dollars in his pocket for the work. He was thirsty, so he bought a soda at a grocery store.

He did not drink it inside. The curb outside was where he was allowed to be, so that is where he sat down with it.

Home was one town over, in Kinloch, then the oldest incorporated Black community in Missouri. He crossed into Ferguson because Ferguson was where the lawns were, and because a boy who wants two dollars goes where the two dollars is.

A police car pulled up while he was sitting there with the bottle. Two officers got out.

They put him against the car and searched him. Then they put handcuffs on a fourteen-year-old for the crime of sitting down after work.

They drove him away from the store. When they let him go they gave him a warning and a slur, and the warning was that he had better not be seen in that town again.

He walked home. Seventy years later he described that afternoon to an interviewer, and he said out loud what he had been thinking on that walk.

He said he could have been another Trayvon Martin.

His mother was in the house. Emma Jean Clay had taught school in Alabama before she married, and she had nine children.

She had picked this one out of the nine to keep beside her until he learned to do something well. He was the fourth.

He told her what had happened on the curb. She did not tell him it would get better.

She told him he would meet racism for the rest of his life, and that he was never to let it become the reason he failed at anything. He was fourteen when she said it, and at ninety-two he was still repeating it word for word.

Here is the second time.

First came Douglass High School, which was segregated, and then Saint Louis University on a scholarship. SLU had opened its doors to Black students only in the summer of 1944, and it admitted five.

That happened because a Jesuit named Claude Heithaus preached against segregation from his own university's pulpit. The university censured him and shipped him out.

Clay graduated in 1951 with a degree in mathematics, among the first Black students that university had ever handed one to. He was twenty-one.

Now he had a piece of paper saying he could do something well. That was the thing his mother had asked of him.

McDonnell Aircraft was in St. Louis, and McDonnell Aircraft wrote to him. They had seen the record, and they invited him in to interview.

So he put on a suit, went across town and gave his name. Then he sat down to wait.

A man came out and took him aside. Not to an office, and not to a desk with a folder on it.

He told him they were very sorry, but they did not have any jobs for him. Clay, telling it more than sixty years afterward, was precise about the reason.

They had not known he was Black until he walked in.

He went home with the degree he had earned and no work in the field he had earned it in. The job he found was teaching school.

Then he taught himself to write software, which in 1951 was a thing almost nobody in the world knew how to do. Five or six years later McDonnell Aircraft called him back and hired him.

He went. If he ever said out loud what that walk back into that building cost him, nobody wrote it down.

Here is the third time.

In 1958 he loaded his wife Virginia and their baby son into a 1956 Ford and drove two thousand three hundred miles to California. It took four days, and he had never in his life been more than five hundred miles from home.

A signed offer was waiting from the Lawrence Radiation Laboratory in Livermore, which the University of California ran for the Atomic Energy Commission. The job was to build a system that tracked radiation after a nuclear explosion.

So a federal weapons laboratory handed him the aftermath of the atomic bomb. Finding somewhere to live was a separate matter.

Nobody in Livermore would rent or sell to a Black family. The man trusted to model nuclear fallout could not sleep near the laboratory that hired him.

So he lived in San Francisco and drove out to Livermore and back every working day. That went on for as long as it took, and he did not quit the job.

Now here is what he built while all of this was going on.

At Control Data he wrote a Fortran compiler. In 1965 David Packard, who wanted Hewlett-Packard in the computer business and had heard there was a man in Palo Alto who knew how, sent for him.

Clay went to the interview and turned the job down flat. Packard called him back personally and told him what he actually wanted built.

Clay came in and started what he called systems programming. There was nothing to copy and nobody who had done it before.

The machine came out of that. It was shown at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco, from the seventh to the tenth of November 1966.

The front panel said Computer in plain letters. The catalog would not say it.

Packard refused the word, because IBM was a customer and twenty times HP's size. So the company sold its first computer as an instrumentation controller and hoped nobody would notice what it was.

In its first year, at most five of them went to anyone outside the company. It was the second sixteen-bit computer offered for sale anywhere in the world, and it sat there.

Then Packard left to run the Pentagon, and Bill Hewlett took over. Hewlett did not want to be in computers at all.

Clay was moved sideways into a position where nobody reported to him and he reported to nobody. That was how Hewlett-Packard got rid of people without ever firing anyone.

He came home and told Virginia. She gave him four words back, and they were that he should not work there.

That same day he called them and quit. When Packard came back from Washington he called again, wanting Clay to return and shut the computer business down.

Clay said no. The two men stood up and shook hands on the end of it.

By 1976, Hewlett-Packard's computer revenue had reached three hundred and forty million dollars, matching everything the instrument business had earned in its entire history. The company he had been asked to help dismantle had become a computer company, and then one of the largest on earth.

In November 2016, that machine turned fifty. Hewlett-Packard had split into four separate corporations by then, and a former HP executive went to the leadership of every one of them about marking the anniversary, and not one of them was interested.

A month later that same man sat in Clay's living room in Piedmont with a recorder running and asked him straight out. In all those years, had the company ever honored the team that started its computer business, with a dinner, a plaque, anything at all.

Clay said he did not recall one.

So we come back to the golf course, because that is where he decided to settle it.

He did not resign from the Olympic Club, and he did not keep his head down inside it. He joined the board, and the members made him president of the golfing side.

In 1992 he became a founding member of the Olympic Club Foundation, which exists to put money into youth sports. Then he sponsored a man named Willie Mays into the club as a special member, which is one way of answering people who took your picture off a wall.

And he started a tournament. The proceeds went to athletics for kids in neighborhoods that had none.

To fill the field he went and got his own people. He called Black friends across the country and told them to come to San Francisco and play.

It grew. One of the club's courses once a year became both of them, twice a year.

By his son's account it was pulling in a few million dollars annually. The money went to children who would never see the inside of that clubhouse.

He found out what the white members called it at a funeral. The club's president had died, and at the service the man's widow told Roy Clay to his face.

They called it the carwash. That was the joke, that once a year the course filled up with Black people.

A group of them went to the club president and asked him to cancel the whole thing. Clay was on the phone when it was put to him.

What he said back was that they were free to get out. He was not leaving.

They did not think he could find enough players to fill a course anyway. So he got back on the phone.

He called, and kept calling, one man at a time across the whole country. That is what you do when nobody is going to do it for you.

On the day of that tournament, a hundred and twenty-five Black golfers stood on the Olympic Club's grass. In a hundred and thirty years there had never been that many on it at once.

Picture him before all of that, though. Picture a man of sixty-something sitting with a telephone and a list of names, making call after call after call, so that a golf course would have to look at them.

That is the same boy off the Ferguson curb, still working. By then he had learned that if you are going to be told you do not belong somewhere, the answer is to arrive with a hundred and twenty-four other people.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.
If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/ssPLXOgFfE
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

Qatari-mediated U.S.-Iran talks made little progress, as both sides refused to compromise and fears of renewed fighting rose.

Qatar proposed linking Iran’s demand to lift the U.S. naval blockade with U.S. demands for nuclear concessions. Iran said it would consider nuclear steps only if Washington returned to the June memorandum of understanding.

U.S. officials initially described the talks as positive and said Trump was open to sanctions relief and the release of frozen funds in exchange for nuclear concessions. Hours later, Trump said he had offered Iran nothing.

A source told Axios the talks were “stuck,” while Trump said Tuesday that Iran “will give up” and “will not have a nuclear weapon.”

text:
Iran offered to reopen Hormuz. Trump said no.
Saturday: Tehran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart peace talks within seven days. Trump rejected it on the spot: "What they wanted is to immediately open the Hormuz Strait... because they have no money coming in."
Now- As I always say---
Read that admission carefully. Trump isn't denying Iran's cash crunch — he's confirming it, and using it as leverage to hold out for more than a reopened strait.
The proposal wasn't new — it echoed June's collapsed MoU, this time reportedly including a US-Oman-Iran transit arrangement Washington hasn't accepted. Hours earlier, Trump posted an image to Truth Social labeling the waterway the "Trump Strait."
Iran's President Pezeshkian, in the same 24 hours, said resolving Hormuz "is possible through negotiations, not the use of force" — but that Tehran doesn't trust talks with Washington. Both sides are negotiating in public, past each other, while a fifth of the world's oil supply sits blocked behind the disagreement.
Renaming a strait doesn't reopen it.

Watch whether the next proposal comes with less rhetoric attached.
